subskill: mode of a data set that has a second, less frequent repeated value
prompt: A player's goal totals in each of 7 games were 13, 6, 16, 6, 10, 13, and 6. What is the mode of these 7 numbers?
explanation: 6 occurs 3 times, 13 occurs twice, and 10 and 16 each occur once, so the mode is 6. 10 is the median, the fourth number once the list is put in order. 13 is the value with the second-highest frequency, which a solver picks after noticing only that some value repeats. 16 is the greatest value in the list.
solve: const v=[13,6,16,6,10,13,6];const c={};for(const x of v)c[x]=(c[x]||0)+1;let best=null;for(const k in c)if(best===null||c[k]>c[best])best=k;return Number(best);

distractor_solve.13: const v=[13,6,16,6,10,13,6];const c={};for(const x of v)c[x]=(c[x]||0)+1;const s=Object.keys(c).sort((a,b)=>c[b]-c[a]);return Number(s[1]);

subskill: range of a data set displayed as a dot plot
prompt: The dot plot shows the number of laps each swimmer on a team completed during one practice. What is the range of the numbers of laps completed?

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Laps completed during one practice, one dot per swimmer.

explanation: The greatest number of laps is 14 and the least is 3, so the range is 14 - 3 = 11. 6 is the value with the most dots above it, the mode rather than the range. 9 comes from overlooking the single dot farthest to the left and subtracting the next value instead, 14 - 5. 14 is the greatest value itself.

distractor_solve.6: const v=[3,5,5,6,6,6,8,8,11,14];const c={};for(const x of v)c[x]=(c[x]||0)+1;let best=null;for(const k in c)if(best===null||c[k]>c[best])best=k;return Number(best);

subskill: probability that a randomly chosen integer is a factor of a given number
prompt: One integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 through 12. What is the probability that the integer chosen is a factor of 24?
explanation: The factors of 24 that lie between 1 and 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12 -- seven of the twelve integers -- so the probability is 7/12. 3/12 counts only the factors of 24 that are greater than 4: 6, 8, and 12. 5/12 counts only the factors strictly between 1 and 12, leaving out both 1 and 12. 6/12 counts the factors of 12 rather than the factors of 24, which drops 8 from the list.

subskill: probability that a randomly drawn numbered tile is prime
prompt: A box contains 20 tiles numbered 1 through 20, and no two tiles carry the same number. One tile is drawn at random. What is the probability that the number on the tile drawn is prime?
explanation: The primes from 1 through 20 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, and 19, so 8 of the 20 tiles qualify and the probability is 8/20 = 2/5. 7/20 leaves out 2, on the belief that an even number cannot be prime. 9/20 counts 1 as a prime. 1/2 counts every odd number, 10 of the 20, as prime.

subskill: probability that one draw from each of two different bags both succeed
prompt: Bag A holds 2 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Bag B holds 4 red marbles and 1 blue marble. One marble is drawn at random from Bag A and one marble is drawn at random from Bag B. What is the probability that both marbles drawn are red?
explanation: The draws are independent, so the probability is (2/5)(4/5) = 8/25. 2/5 is the probability that the marble from Bag A alone is red, which ignores Bag B entirely. 3/5 pools all 10 marbles and reports the 6 red ones as a single fraction. 17/25 is the probability that the two marbles are NOT both red.

subskill: probability of a union of two overlapping events on one roll
prompt: A fair 8-sided die has faces numbered 1 through 8. The die is rolled once. What is the probability that the number rolled is even OR greater than 5?
explanation: The numbers that are even or greater than 5 are 2, 4, 6, 7, and 8 -- five of the eight faces -- so the probability is 5/8. 3/8 counts only 6, 7, and 8, the numbers greater than 5. 1/2 counts only the four even numbers. 7/8 adds the 4 even faces and the 3 faces greater than 5 without removing 6 and 8, which were counted twice.

subskill: counting principle over three independent choices
prompt: A deli offers 5 kinds of bread, 4 kinds of meat, and 3 kinds of cheese. A sandwich is made with exactly one kind of bread, one kind of meat, and one kind of cheese. How many different sandwiches can be made?
explanation: Each of the 5 breads can be paired with each of the 4 meats and each of the 3 cheeses, so there are 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 sandwiches. 12 adds the three counts, 5 + 4 + 3, instead of multiplying them. 20 is 5 x 4, the count after the bread and the meat but before the cheese. 27 is (5 + 4) x 3, adding the bread and meat counts before multiplying by the cheeses.

subskill: geometric probability from a ratio of areas
prompt: A square dartboard measures 10 inches on each side. A shaded square region measuring 4 inches on each side lies entirely inside the dartboard. A dart lands at a random point on the dartboard. What is the probability that the dart lands in the shaded region?
explanation: The shaded area is 4 x 4 = 16 square inches out of 10 x 10 = 100 square inches, so the probability is 16/100 = 4/25. 2/5 compares the side lengths, 4 to 10, instead of the areas. 3/5 compares the part of a side outside the shaded square, 10 - 4, to the whole side. 21/25 is the probability that the dart lands outside the shaded region.

subskill: correcting one mis-recorded value and recomputing the mean
prompt: The mean weight of the 10 packages in a shipment was recorded as 74 ounces. Later it was found that one package's weight had been entered as 58 ounces when the package actually weighed 88 ounces. All other entries were correct. What is the correct mean weight, in ounces, of the 10 packages?
explanation: The recorded total was 10 x 74 = 740 ounces. Replacing 58 with 88 raises the total by 30, to 770, so the correct mean is 770/10 = 77. 71 subtracts the 3-ounce correction from the mean instead of adding it. 74 assumes one changed entry cannot move the mean. 104 adds the whole 30-ounce difference to the mean rather than to the total.

subskill: probability that two draws without replacement give different colors
prompt: A jar holds 6 red chips and 4 blue chips and nothing else. Two chips are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. What is the probability that the two chips drawn are different colors?
explanation: Red then blue has probability (6/10)(4/9) and blue then red has probability (4/10)(6/9), so together the probability is 48/90 = 8/15. 1/3 is the probability that both chips are red, one of the two matching cases. 7/15 is the probability that the two chips MATCH in color. 12/25 computes the same two orders as if the first chip had been put back, using 2(6/10)(4/10).

subskill: probability of exactly one of two overlapping events from group counts
prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 play soccer, 14 play tennis, and 6 play both soccer and tennis. One student from the class is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student plays exactly one of the two sports?
explanation: Soccer only accounts for 18 - 6 = 12 students and tennis only for 14 - 6 = 8, so 20 of the 30 students play exactly one sport and the probability is 20/30 = 2/3. 2/15 is the probability that the student plays neither sport, since 18 + 14 - 6 = 26 play at least one. 1/5 is the probability that the student plays both. 2/5 counts only the 12 students who play soccer and not tennis.

subskill: total probability across two kinds of coin
prompt: A box holds 3 coins: 2 of them are fair, and 1 has heads on both sides. One coin is taken from the box at random and flipped once. What is the probability that the coin lands heads up?
explanation: A fair coin is taken with probability 2/3 and then lands heads with probability 1/2, and the two-headed coin is taken with probability 1/3 and lands heads with probability 1, so the total is (2/3)(1/2) + (1/3)(1) = 2/3. 1/2 treats every coin in the box as fair. 3/4 averages the two kinds of coin, (1/2 + 1)/2, as though there were one of each rather than two fair coins and one two-headed coin. 5/6 adds 1/2 and 1/3 instead of weighting each coin by how likely it is to be chosen.

subskill: percent of a distribution at or above a value, read from a bar graph
prompt: The bar graph shows how many books each student in one class read last month. What percent of the students in the class read 3 or more books?

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Books read last month, by number of students.

explanation: The bars total 6 + 9 + 12 + 9 + 6 + 6 = 48 students, and 9 + 6 + 6 = 21 of them read 3 or more books, so the percent is 21/48 = 43.75%. 25% counts only the students who read MORE than 3 books, leaving out the ones who read exactly 3. 56.25% is the percent who read fewer than 3 books. 75% is the percent who read 3 or FEWER books, reading the inequality in the other direction.

subskill: recovering a missing table cell from the margins, then a joint probability
prompt: The table shows how the people at a community meeting answered one survey question. One of the people at the meeting is chosen at random. What is the probability that the person chosen is an adult who answered No?

graphic.caption: Figure 1. Survey responses. One cell is not shown.

explanation: The missing cell is 80 - 30 = 50 adults who answered No, out of 200 people in all, so the probability is 50/200 = 1/4. 7/20 uses the adults who answered Yes, 70 of 200. 2/5 uses the No column total, 80 of 200, without separating the adults from the students. 5/12 is the probability of answering No GIVEN that the person is an adult, 50 of 120, which conditions on the adults instead of on everyone at the meeting.

subskill: probability that the sum of two dice is at or above a value
prompt: Two fair 6-sided dice, each with faces numbered 1 through 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers rolled is 8 or more?
explanation: Of the 36 equally likely rolls, 5 give a sum of 8, 4 give 9, 3 give 10, 2 give 11, and 1 gives 12, for 15 rolls in all, so the probability is 15/36. 10/36 counts only the sums greater than 8, leaving out the sums of 8 that the question asks to include. 21/36 is the probability that the sum is 7 or less. 26/36 is the probability that the sum is 8 or LESS, reading the inequality in the other direction.

subskill: mean of a run of consecutive integers
prompt: What is the mean of the integers from 12 through 40, inclusive?
explanation: The integers are evenly spaced, so their mean is the average of the first and last, (12 + 40)/2 = 26. 28 is 40 - 12, the range of the list rather than its mean. 29 is 40 - 12 + 1, the number of integers in the list. 32 comes from writing 12 + 40/2, halving only the greater value instead of halving the sum.

subskill: overall percent combining two groups of different sizes
prompt: A factory received 120 motors from supplier A, of which 18 were defective, and 280 motors from supplier B, of which 14 were defective. What percent of all the motors the factory received were defective?
explanation: There were 18 + 14 = 32 defective motors out of 120 + 280 = 400 received, so 32/400 = 8% were defective. 4.5% counts only supplier A's 18 defective motors against all 400 received. 10% averages the two suppliers' own rates, 15% and 5%, without weighting them by how many motors each supplier sent. 20% adds those two rates instead of combining them.

subskill: which value can be removed without changing the mean
prompt: Consider the data set 3, 8, 9, 11, 24. Removing which one of these values leaves the remaining four values with the same mean as all five values had?
explanation: All five values have mean 55/5 = 11, and removing a value equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged: 44/4 = 11. Removing 3 leaves 52/4 = 13. Removing 9, the median, leaves 46/4 = 11.5. Removing 24, the greatest value, leaves 31/4 = 7.75.

subskill: upper outlier boundary from the 1.5 times IQR rule
prompt: For a data set, the first quartile Q1 is the median of the lower half of the values and the third quartile Q3 is the median of the upper half, and the interquartile range is IQR = Q3 - Q1. A value is called an outlier if it is greater than Q3 + 1.5(IQR) or less than Q1 - 1.5(IQR). For the data set 8, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 42, what is the value of Q3 + 1.5(IQR)?
explanation: The lower half is 8, 12, 14, 15, so Q1 = (12 + 14)/2 = 13, and the upper half is 17, 18, 19, 42, so Q3 = (18 + 19)/2 = 18.5. Then IQR = 5.5 and Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 18.5 + 8.25 = 26.75. 29.5 takes the quartiles to be the data values 12 and 19 rather than the medians of the two halves, giving 19 + 1.5(19 - 12). 34.25 measures the spread from the least value up to Q3, 18.5 - 8, and uses that in place of the IQR. 69.5 uses the range, 42 - 8 = 34, in place of the IQR.

subskill: probability that the first success occurs on a stated trial
prompt: A weighted coin lands heads up with probability 2/5 on each flip, and the flips are independent. The coin is flipped repeatedly. What is the probability that the first flip to land heads up is the third flip?
explanation: The first two flips must land tails, each with probability 3/5, and the third must land heads, with probability 2/5, so the probability is (3/5)(3/5)(2/5) = 18/125. 27/125 is the probability that none of the first three flips lands heads. 50/125 is 2/5, the probability that the third flip lands heads on its own, which ignores what the first two flips must do. 98/125 is the probability that at least one of the first three flips lands heads.

subskill: probability of at least two successes in four fair flips
prompt: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. What is the probability that the coin lands heads up at least 2 times?
explanation: Of the 16 equally likely sequences of 4 flips, 6 have exactly 2 heads, 4 have exactly 3, and 1 has 4, so 11 sequences have at least 2 heads and the probability is 11/16. 4/16 is the probability of exactly 3 heads. 5/16 is the probability of FEWER than 2 heads, the complement that has been computed but not subtracted from 1. 15/16 is the probability of at least 1 head, answering for a threshold of 1 instead of 2.

subskill: solving for the probability that makes a game break even
prompt: In a carnival game a player pays $3 to play. With probability p the player wins and is handed $10; otherwise the player is handed nothing. For what value of p is the player's expected net gain equal to $0?
explanation: A win nets 10 - 3 = 7 dollars and a loss nets -3 dollars, so the expected net gain is 7p - 3(1 - p) = 10p - 3, which is 0 when p = 3/10. 3/13 divides the $3 cost by $13, the cost plus the prize, instead of by the prize. 7/10 is 1 - 3/10, the probability of LOSING at the break-even value of p. 7/13 puts the $7 net win over that same $13 total.

subskill: committees meeting an at-least-one requirement, counted by complement
prompt: A committee of 3 people is to be chosen from a group of 4 teachers and 5 students. How many different committees include at least 1 teacher?
explanation: There are 84 committees of 3 from the 9 people, and 10 of them are made up of students only, so 84 - 10 = 74 include at least 1 teacher. 30 counts only the committees with exactly 2 teachers, 6 pairs of teachers times 5 students. 40 counts only the committees with exactly 1 teacher, 4 teachers times 10 pairs of students. 84 is every committee of 3, ignoring the requirement.
solve: const C=(n,k)=>{let r=1;for(let i=0;i<k;i++)r=r*(n-i)/(i+1);return Math.round(r);};return C(9,3)-C(5,3);

subskill: counting selections from a row with no two adjacent
prompt: Ten chairs are arranged in a single row. Four of the chairs are to be chosen so that no two chosen chairs are next to each other. In how many ways can the four chairs be chosen?
explanation: Line up the 6 chairs that are not chosen; they create 7 gaps (including the two ends), and choosing 4 of those gaps for the chosen chairs guarantees no two are adjacent, so there are 35 ways. 15 comes from choosing 4 gaps out of 6, subtracting the number of chairs chosen rather than one less than that. 126 comes from setting one chair aside to account for the restriction and then choosing 4 chairs freely from the remaining 9. 210 is every choice of 4 chairs from 10, ignoring the restriction.
solve: const C=(n,k)=>{let r=1;for(let i=0;i<k;i++)r=r*(n-i)/(i+1);return Math.round(r);};return C(7,4);
